title: Research
text:
Research
    
      Selected work across theoretical neuroscience, large-scale brain
      dynamics, and biologically inspired learning.
    
  

  
    Selected work
    
      
        
          
        
        
          Graduate Summer Research
          Serial Dependence in Visual Working Memory
          
            New York University Shanghai
            Jun–Aug 2026
          
          Advisor: Sukbin Lim
          
            
              I studied how recent and more distant experiences shape current
              visual working-memory representations. I developed a computational
              model combining history-dependent efficient coding with
              attractor-based memory to investigate the coexistence of attractive
              and repulsive serial biases across different timescales.
            
            
              The model qualitatively reproduced short-term attraction and
              longer-range repulsion under short-delay conditions, while
              delay-dependent discrepancies motivated further exploration of
              multiscale history effects and memory uncertainty.
            
          
        
      

      
        
          
        
        
          Research Project
          Large-Scale Network Dynamics during Working Memory
          
            Westlake University
            Apr 2025–May 2026
          
          Advisor: Yuchen Xiao
          
            
              I investigated how distributed brain networks coordinate during
              working-memory recognition, encoding, and retrieval using
              intracranial recordings from 1,652 sites across 36 patients.
            
            
              I analyzed cross-frequency coupling and directed information flow
              to characterize large-scale interactions across different stages of
              working memory. My primary contribution was developing and applying
              a time-delay embedded hidden Markov model (TDE-HMM) to identify
              time-resolved latent network states and characterize their dynamics
              during working-memory processing. This work contributed to a
              bioRxiv preprint on frontotemporal network dynamics during
              working-memory processing.
            
          
          View preprint ↗
        
      

      
        
          
        
        
          Undergraduate Thesis
          Multiscale Dynamics of Functional Ultrasound Hemodynamics
          
            Xi'an Jiaotong University
            Jan–Jun 2026
          
          Advisors: Junjie Jiang and Zhiqiang Wei
          
            
              For my undergraduate thesis, I studied multiscale hemodynamic
              changes in a rat neuroinflammation dataset using functional
              ultrasound imaging. I characterized changes in spectral activity,
              functional connectivity, long-range temporal dependence, and
              low-dimensional network structure across experimental conditions.
            
            
              I further developed a delayed coupled-oscillator model with a
              vascular observation layer and used approximate Bayesian computation
              to relate changes in observed hemodynamics to interpretable
              dynamical parameters.
            
          
        
      

      
        
          
        
        
          Independent Research
          Biologically Inspired Learning for Monocular Depth Estimation
          
            Jun–Oct 2024
          
          
            
              I explored whether biologically inspired Hebbian learning could be
              incorporated into modern computer-vision architectures. I developed
              a hybrid ResNet–U-Net model with a SoftHebb layer that adapted
              intermediate feature representations through co-activation-based
              updates for monocular depth estimation.
            
            
              This work resulted in my first research publication and helped shape
              my later interest in the relationship between biological and
              artificial learning.
            
          
          View publication ↗

title: Contact
text:
Collaborate
    
      I am interested in a wide range of collaborations.
    
  

  
    Directions
    
      
        I am particularly interested in collaborations across three broad
        directions:
      

      
        
          Interdisciplinary Neuroscience
          
            Exploring connections between neuroscience and other fields,
            including art, embodied intelligence, and unconventional ways of
            studying or applying principles of the brain.
          
        

        
          Theory × Experiment
          
            Working with experimental neuroscientists to connect computational
            and theoretical ideas with neural and behavioral data, and to
            develop questions that can be tested in biological systems.
          
        

        
          NeuroAI
          
            Exploring how principles discovered in biological intelligence
            might inform artificial systems—and how artificial systems, in
            turn, might help us better understand the brain.
          
        
      

      
        If any of these directions overlap with your interests, feel free to
        reach out by email. I am always
        happy to discuss potential ideas and collaborations.
      
    
  

  
    Elsewhere
    
      
        Outside research, I occasionally share glimpses of everyday life,
        travel, art, and things I find interesting.

title: About
text:
About
    
      I am a Ph.D. student in Neural Science at New York University, working
      with Prof. Sukbin Lim. My interests lie broadly in theoretical
      neuroscience and NeuroAI.
    
  

  
    Research
    
      From memory to intelligence.
      
        I am fascinated by how human memories are formed, stored, and
        transformed within the human brain. More broadly, I am interested in
        whether the simple computational principles we uncover in the brain
        can help us understand intelligence and inspire better artificial
        systems.
      
      
        At the broadest level, these questions connect to what has always
        fascinated me most: how physical neural processes give rise to the
        mind, the self, and conscious experience.
